lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you met the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971. What does it do? (It puts illegal drugs into classes A, B and C.) Today: alcohol, vaping, the law, and peer pressure.

Alcohol is a drug that slows the brain and body: balance, judgement, memory and reactions. The brain keeps developing until about 25, so young people are hit harder. The UK's top doctors advise an alcohol-free childhood.

In the UK it is against the law to sell alcohol, tobacco or vapes to anyone under 18. Adults must not buy alcohol for them either. Police can take alcohol from under-18s in public, and single-use vapes are banned from sale.
Vapes usually contain nicotine, which is addictive: the body craves more, so it is hard to stop. Vapes are meant only to help adults stop smoking. Smoking harms the heart and lungs.

Peer pressure can be direct, when someone asks or dares you. It can be indirect, when everyone seems to be doing it, or come from inside, like wanting to fit in. Most young people your age don't drink, smoke or vape.
Ways to say no: a clear 'No thanks', a reason, another idea, humour, saying it again, or walking away. Agree a code word with a parent that means 'come and get me'. Real friends accept a no.

Getting help: a trusted adult, your GP or the school nurse. FRANK gives free, confidential advice on drugs on 0300 123 6600, and Childline is on 0800 1111. If someone is very unwell, call 999 and stay with them.

Try it in the world: agree a code word with a grown-up, and practise a 'No thanks' with a friend. In LIFE, Calm Corner practises saying no to pressure, and the Poisons Cupboard keeps medicines and chemicals safe. Next: CPR and defibrillators.

exercises.prompt: In the UK, shops must not sell alcohol to anyone under 18.
exercises.hint: Think of the age in the law table.
exercises.explain: True: it is against the law to sell alcohol to anyone under 18.

exercises.prompt: Which substance in most vapes is addictive?
exercises.hint: Which one makes the body crave more?
exercises.explain: Nicotine is addictive, which is why vapes are only for adults trying to stop smoking.

items: a dare in front of the group
everyone in the photos seems to drink
exercises.hint: Is a person asking, is it the crowd, or is it your own feeling?
exercises.explain: Direct: a dare, an offer. Indirect: what others seem to do. From inside: wanting to look older, worrying.

exercises.prompt: Most young people your age don't drink alcohol, smoke or vape.
exercises.hint: Think about what most people really do, not what seems to happen.
exercises.explain: True: most young people don't, so saying no is normal.

exercises.prompt: What do the UK's top doctors advise for children and alcohol?
exercises.hint: Think about how alcohol affects a brain that is still growing.
exercises.explain: Because the brain keeps developing until about 25, the advice is no alcohol at all in childhood.

exercises.prompt: Match each way of saying no to an example.
exercises.explain: A reason, another idea, saying it again, and a code word: all clear ways to say no.

exercises.prompt: The brain keeps developing until about 25. How many more years is that for a 13-year-old?
exercises.explain: 25 − 13 = 12 more years of the brain developing.

exercises.prompt: A friend offers you a vape on the way home. What is a strong reply?
choices: 'No thanks. Let's go to the park.'
'I'll take it and bin it later.'
exercises.hint: Which reply is clear and changes the plan?
exercises.explain: A clear no plus another idea ends the offer without a long argument.

exercises.prompt: An adult can legally buy alcohol for a 15-year-old to drink in the park.
exercises.hint: Think about the law on buying for under-18s, and alcohol in public.
exercises.explain: False: buying alcohol for an under-18 is against the law, and police can take alcohol from under-18s in public.

exercises.prompt: Put a strong refusal in order.
items: give a reason, if you want
exercises.hint: Say it, back it up, change the plan, leave, then talk to someone.
exercises.explain: No thanks, a reason, another idea, walk away, and later tell a trusted adult.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of pressure is 'everyone at the party seems to be drinking'?
exercises.explain: Nobody asks you directly: it is the crowd's example, so it is indirect pressure.

exercises.prompt: FRANK's number is 0300 123 6600. How many digits does it have?
exercises.hint: Count every digit, including the zeros.

exercises.prompt: At a party, friends keep asking after you have said no. What is the best plan?
choices: leave, and text your code word home
exercises.hint: Which choice gets you safely out?
exercises.explain: Leaving and texting the code word gets a grown-up to collect you, without any argument.

exercises.prompt: A cold shower or strong coffee sobers someone up who has drunk too much.
exercises.hint: What really happens to alcohol in the body?
exercises.explain: False: only time clears alcohol. If someone is very unwell, call 999, put them in the recovery position if they are breathing, and stay with them.

items: alcohol keeps you warm in the cold
vapes are made for young people
exercises.hint: Think of the lesson's facts about nicotine, alcohol and the brain.
exercises.explain: True: nicotine is addictive, alcohol slows the brain, the brain develops until 25. Myths: vapes for young people, alcohol keeps you warm.

exercises.prompt: Who can give free, confidential advice about drugs in the UK?
exercises.hint: The lesson named a service and its number.
exercises.explain: FRANK gives free, confidential advice; Childline (0800 1111) and trusted adults can help too.
